title: Yes, no and questions
can_do: You can ask and answer yes/no questions.

grammar.heading: Yes and no
grammar.body: `haaN` is "yes" and `nahiiN` is "no". With elders and anyone you don't know well, put `jii` in front: `jii haaN`, `jii nahiiN`. A plain `jii` is also a polite "yes". Plain `haaN` is fine with friends.

grammar.heading: "Not": `nahiiN` before the verb
grammar.body: To say "not", put `nahiiN` straight before the verb at the end. Nothing else changes. In everyday speech the verb is often dropped after `nahiiN`: `maiN doctor nahiiN` means the same as `maiN doctor nahiiN huuN`.

grammar.heading: Questions: `kyaa` at the start
grammar.body: Any sentence becomes a yes/no question if your voice goes up at the end: `aap tayyaar haiN?` To make it clearly a question, put `kyaa` at the start. Here `kyaa` doesn't mean "what"; it just marks the question, a bit like "do" or "is" in English. The word order stays the same.

examples.en: Is he a student? / Is she a student?

grammar.heading: Short answers
grammar.body: You don't have to answer in a full sentence. `zaruur` ("of course") makes a keen yes, `shaayad` is "maybe", and `pataa nahiiN` is "no idea".

exercises.prompt: Imran, your neighbour, asks you this. You are ready. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: `jii haaN` is the polite "yes". Imran is older than you, so the `jii` matters.
Build the sentence as usual, then slot `nahiiN` in just before the verb.

exercises.instruction: Make it a clear yes/no question with `kyaa`.
exercises.explanation: Put `kyaa` at the start. Nothing else moves.

exercises.instruction: Make it negative: we're not ready.
exercises.explanation: `nahiiN` goes before `haiN`. Dropping `haiN` after `nahiiN` is just as natural.
`nahiiN` goes right before the verb, not after `maiN`.
The verb is `ho`, which only goes with `tum`.
`kyaa` at the start makes it a question. `wo` could just as well be "he".

exercises.prompt: In this question, what does `kyaa` do?
options: It just marks a yes/no question
exercises.explanation: At the start of a sentence, `kyaa` simply signals a yes/no question. In `kyaa haal hai?` it does mean "what".

exercises.prompt: A neighbour asks if the community centre is open today. You've no idea. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: `pataa nahiiN` is "no idea"; the `jii` in front keeps it polite.

exercises.en: No, I'm not a doctor. I'm a student.
